subQuestions.questionText: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH is:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — butan-1-ol (2 marks)
4-carbon chain (butan-) with –OH on C1; the principal chain is numbered to give the OH the lowest locant.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following compounds has the HIGHEST boiling point?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — pentanoic acid (2 marks)
The –COOH group enables strong hydrogen bonding (and, in carboxylic acids, dimer formation) plus dipole-dipole interactions, giving the highest boiling point of the four.

subQuestions.questionText: The functional group of an ester is:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — ─COO─ (2 marks)
The ester linkage forms between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (R–COO–R′).

subQuestions.questionText: In the reaction CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O, the type of reaction is:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — elimination (2 marks)
A hydrogen and a hydroxyl group are removed from adjacent carbons of ethanol to form an alkene plus water (dehydration).

subQuestions.questionText: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, increasing pressure in the equilibrium N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ will:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — shift equilibrium to the right (2 marks)
The right-hand side has fewer moles of gas (2 mol NH₃ vs 4 mol of N₂ + H₂); increased pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.

subQuestions.questionText: A buffer solution resists changes in pH because it contains:

options.B: a strong acid and its salt
options.C: a weak acid and its conjugate base

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — a weak acid and its conjugate base (2 marks)
A buffer contains a weak acid/conjugate base pair (or weak base/conjugate acid) which neutralises small additions of either H⁺ or OH⁻.

subQuestions.questionText: In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — anode (2 marks)
Definition: oxidation (loss of electrons) always occurs at the anode in any electrochemical cell.

subQuestions.questionText: The standard electrode potential (E°) of Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V and Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V. The E°cell is:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — +1.10 V (2 marks)
$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10$ V.

subQuestions.questionText: During the electrolysis of dilute H₂SO₄, the gas produced at the cathode is:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B — H₂ (2 marks)
Reduction at the cathode: $2H^+ + 2e^- \to H_2$. Oxygen is produced at the anode.

subQuestions.questionText: Which of the following is a STRONG acid?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C — HNO₃ (2 marks)
Nitric acid fully (≈100%) dissociates in water. The other three are weak acids that only partially dissociate.

questions.title: Organic Chemistry — Naming, Isomerism and Properties

subQuestions.questionText: The following compound is given: CH₃─CH₂─CH₂─CH₂─CH₂─OH. Write the IUPAC name of this compound.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 5-carbon straight chain with –OH on carbon 1.
Mark 2: IUPAC name: pentan-1-ol.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the name of the functional group.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Hydroxyl group (–OH).

subQuestions.questionText: To which homologous series does this compound belong?
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Alcohols (alkanols) / primary alcohols.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the general formula for this homologous series.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$ (or equivalent $C_nH_{2n+2}O$).

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the molecular formula of this compound.
Draw the structural formula of a CHAIN ISOMER of this compound.
subQuestions.memoText:
A correct chain isomer must be drawn — same molecular formula ($C_5H_{12}O$) but a different (branched) carbon skeleton, still containing –OH.
Mark 1: Branched 5-carbon chain (different skeleton).
Mark 2: Correct number of H atoms (saturated, no double bonds).
Mark 3: –OH group present and shown clearly.
Acceptable examples: 2-methylbutan-1-ol — $CH_3CH(CH_3)CH_2CH_2OH$; 3-methylbutan-1-ol — $(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_2OH$; 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol — $(CH_3)_3CCH_2OH$.

subQuestions.questionText: Draw the structural formula of a POSITIONAL ISOMER of this compound.
subQuestions.memoText:
A correct positional isomer — same straight 5-carbon chain but with –OH on a different carbon.
Mark 1: Straight 5-carbon chain (same skeleton as pentan-1-ol).
Mark 2: –OH attached to C2 or C3 (not C1).
Mark 3: All bonds drawn correctly (full structural formula).
Acceptable examples: pentan-2-ol — $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_2CH_3$; pentan-3-ol — $CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_2CH_3$.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC name of each isomer you drew in 2.6 and 2.7.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Correct IUPAC name for the chain isomer in 2.6 (e.g. 2-methylbutan-1-ol or 3-methylbutan-1-ol or 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol).
Mark 2: Correct IUPAC name for the positional isomer in 2.7 (e.g. pentan-2-ol or pentan-3-ol).
[Names must match the structures drawn.]

subQuestions.questionText: Which compound has the higher boiling point — this compound or its chain isomer? Explain your answer in terms of intermolecular forces.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Pentan-1-ol (the straight-chain compound) has the HIGHER boiling point.
Mark 2: Both compounds have the same types of intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding via –OH plus London/dispersion forces) and the same molar mass.
Mark 3: Pentan-1-ol has a longer, unbranched chain → larger surface area for contact between molecules → stronger London/dispersion forces.
Mark 4: The branched chain isomer has a more compact shape → smaller contact surface → weaker London forces → lower boiling point.

subQuestions.questionText: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of this compound.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Reactants and products correctly identified: $C_5H_{12}O + O_2 \to CO_2 + H_2O$.
Mark 2: Correct stoichiometry: $2C_5H_{12}O + 15O_2 \to 10CO_2 + 12H_2O$ (or equivalent fractional form $C_5H_{12}O + \tfrac{15}{2}O_2 \to 5CO_2 + 6H_2O$).
Mark 3: Equation fully balanced (atoms balanced on both sides).

subQuestions.questionText: Consider the following substances: water (H₂O), hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), ethane (C₂H₆), and ethanol (C₂H₅OH). Identify the type(s) of intermolecular forces present in: (a) water, (b) ethane, (c) ethanol.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (a) Water: hydrogen bonding (plus dipole-dipole and London/dispersion forces).
Mark 2 (b) Ethane: London/dispersion forces ONLY (non-polar molecule).
Mark 3 (c) Ethanol: hydrogen bonding (plus dipole-dipole and London/dispersion forces).
Mark 4: Awarded for correctly distinguishing that only the molecules containing –OH (water, ethanol) exhibit hydrogen bonding, while ethane (purely non-polar C–C and C–H bonds) does not.

subQuestions.questionText: Arrange the following in order of INCREASING boiling point: H₂S, H₂O, CH₄. Explain your reasoning.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Order of increasing boiling point: $CH_4 < H_2S < H_2O$.
Mark 2: $CH_4$ — non-polar; only weak London/dispersion forces → lowest boiling point (≈ −161 °C).
Mark 3: $H_2S$ — polar; dipole-dipole + London forces (intermediate strength) → intermediate boiling point (≈ −60 °C).
Mark 4: $H_2O$ — strong hydrogen bonding → highest boiling point (+100 °C). Despite $H_2O$ having a lower molar mass than $H_2S$, hydrogen bonds are much stronger than dipole-dipole forces.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why ethanol is miscible with water but hexane is not.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Ethanol contains an –OH group and is polar; it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules → fully miscible with water.
‘Like dissolves like’ — both ethanol and water are polar and can form similar IMFs.
Mark 2: Hexane is non-polar (only London/dispersion forces between molecules).
Mark 3: Hexane cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and the energy released from hexane–water interactions is too small to overcome the strong water–water hydrogen bonds → hexane is immiscible with water.

subQuestions.questionText: Write the IUPAC names and structural formulae of the TWO products when butan-1-ol undergoes an elimination reaction (dehydration). State the conditions required.
subQuestions.memoText:
Elimination/dehydration of butan-1-ol gives a mixture of alkenes:
Mark 1: Product 1 structure: $CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$
Mark 2: Product 1 name: but-1-ene
Mark 3: Product 2 structure: $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$
Mark 4: Product 2 name: but-2-ene
Mark 5: Conditions — concentrated $H_2SO_4$ (or $H_3PO_4$) as acid catalyst.
Mark 6: Conditions — heat, approximately 170 °C.
[Water $(H_2O)$ is also produced as a by-product.]

subQuestions.questionText: Write a balanced equation for the esterification reaction between ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH). Name the ester formed and state the conditions.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Correct reactants on the left of the equation: $C_2H_5OH + CH_3CH_2COOH$.
Mark 2: Correct ester product: $CH_3CH_2COOC_2H_5$.
Mark 3: Water as second product and equation written as a reversible equilibrium: $C_2H_5OH + CH_3CH_2COOH \rightleftharpoons CH_3CH_2COOC_2H_5 + H_2O$.
Mark 4: Ester name: ethyl propanoate.
Mark 5: Conditions — concentrated $H_2SO_4$ catalyst, heat gently / under reflux.

subQuestions.questionText: Bromine water is added to two test tubes — one containing hexane and one containing hex-1-ene. Describe and explain what is observed in each test tube.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Hexane: NO change — bromine water remains orange/brown (or red-brown).
Mark 2: Reason: hexane is a saturated alkane (no C=C double bond) and does not react with $Br_2$ under these conditions.
Mark 3: Hex-1-ene: bromine water DECOLOURISES (turns colourless).
Mark 4: Reason: $Br_2$ adds across the C=C double bond in an addition reaction: $CH_2=CH–R + Br_2 \to CH_2Br–CHBr–R$. This is the standard test that distinguishes alkenes from alkanes.

subQuestions.questionText: Write a balanced equation for the addition reaction of HBr with propene (CH₃CH=CH₂). Name the product.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Reactants and products written: $CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \to$ product.
Mark 2: Major product structure (Markovnikov's rule — H adds to the C with more H's, Br to the more substituted C): $CH_3CHBrCH_3$.
Mark 3: Equation balanced: $CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \to CH_3CHBrCH_3$.
Mark 4: Major product name: 2-bromopropane.
[Accept 1-bromopropane $(CH_3CH_2CH_2Br)$ as the minor anti-Markovnikov product if clearly identified.]

subQuestions.questionText: Marble chips (CaCO₃) react with hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). The graphs in the question paper show the effect of conditions on the rate. Define the term "reaction rate". (Refer to the concentration-vs-time and Maxwell-Boltzmann graphs in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Reaction rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
Mark 2: Stated mathematically as $\text{rate} = \Delta[\text{concentration}]/\Delta t$, with units mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain, using collision theory, why increasing temperature increases reaction rate.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Higher temperature → particles have greater (average) kinetic energy and move faster.
Mark 2: A greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy ($E_a$).
Mark 3: The collision frequency also increases. Therefore the number of effective (successful) collisions per second increases → reaction rate increases.

subQuestions.questionText: A catalyst is added to the reaction. What is the effect on: (a) the activation energy, and (b) the value of ΔH? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: (a) Activation energy DECREASES.
Mark 2: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater fraction of particles have sufficient energy to react.
Mark 3: (b) $\Delta H$ is UNCHANGED.
Mark 4: A catalyst does not alter the energy of the reactants or products — it only lowers the energy barrier between them; therefore the enthalpy difference $\Delta H = H_\text{products} - H_\text{reactants}$ is unaffected.

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO other ways to increase the rate of this reaction and explain each using collision theory.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid methods (other than catalyst/temperature):
Method 1 — Increase concentration of HCl (Marks 1–2): More acid particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions per second → more successful collisions per second → faster rate.
Method 2 — Increase surface area of $CaCO_3$ (use powder instead of chips) (Marks 3–4): Greater surface exposed to acid → more $CaCO_3$ particles available for collision → more frequent collisions → faster rate.
[Other acceptable answers: stirring (improves contact between reactants).]

subQuestions.questionText: Sketch the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and show how adding a catalyst shifts the effective threshold. Label axes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Axes correctly labelled — x-axis: energy (E); y-axis: number of particles (or fraction of particles).
Mark 2: Bell-shaped Maxwell-Boltzmann curve drawn (rising from origin, peak, then long tail to the right).
Mark 3: Vertical dashed line marking the activation energy $E_a$ (without catalyst), and a SECOND vertical dashed line for $E_a$ (with catalyst) shifted to the LEFT of the original.
Mark 4: Shaded area under the curve to the right of $E_a$ — clearly LARGER for the catalysed $E_a$ (more particles have $E \geq E_a$ when a catalyst is present).

subQuestions.questionText: Consider the following equilibrium reaction at 400°C: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) ΔH = −92 kJ·mol⁻¹. (Refer to the concentration-vs-time graph in the question paper.) Write the expression for the equilibrium constant Kc for this reaction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Numerator (products) raised to correct stoichiometric power: $[NH_3]^2$.
Mark 2: Denominator (reactants) with correct powers: $[N_2][H_2]^3$.
$K_c = \dfrac{[NH_3]^2}{[N_2][H_2]^3}$

subQuestions.questionText: The equilibrium concentrations are: [N₂] = 0.50 mol·dm⁻³, [H₂] = 1.50 mol·dm⁻³, [NH₃] = 0.80 mol·dm⁻³. Calculate Kc.
State Le Chatelier's Principle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change (in concentration, temperature or pressure)...
Mark 2: ...the system will shift in the direction that opposes/counteracts the change and re-establishes equilibrium.

subQuestions.questionText: State the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of NH₃. Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Equilibrium shifts to the LEFT (toward reactants); yield of $NH_3$ DECREASES.
Mark 2: The forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H = -92$ kJ·mol⁻¹). Increasing temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction to absorb the added heat.

subQuestions.questionText: State the effect of increasing the pressure on the equilibrium yield of NH₃. Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Equilibrium shifts to the RIGHT (toward products); yield of $NH_3$ INCREASES.
Mark 2: The right-hand side has fewer moles of gas (2 mol) than the left (4 mol). By Le Chatelier's principle, increased pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas.

subQuestions.questionText: State the effect of adding a catalyst on the equilibrium yield of NH₃. Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: NO change in the equilibrium position or in the yield of $NH_3$.
Mark 2: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached FASTER but the same $K_c$ (and hence yield) applies.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why an increase in temperature causes the value of Kc for this reaction to DECREASE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction (Le Chatelier).
Mark 2: This shifts the equilibrium to the LEFT — at the new equilibrium $[NH_3]$ is lower while $[N_2]$ and $[H_2]$ are higher.
Mark 3: Since $K_c = [NH_3]^2 / ([N_2][H_2]^3)$, the numerator decreases and the denominator increases, so $K_c$ DECREASES.

subQuestions.questionText: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH is titrated with 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ HCl. Define an acid according to the Brønsted-Lowry theory.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton ($H^+$) donor...
Mark 2: ...i.e. a substance that donates a proton to another substance (the base).

subQuestions.questionText: Write the balanced ionic equation for the neutralisation reaction between NaOH and HCl.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Correct reactant ions: $H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq)$.
Mark 2: Correct product and balanced equation: $H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \to H_2O(\ell)$.
[Accept also $H_3O^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \to 2H_2O(\ell)$.]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the volume of HCl needed to exactly neutralise the NaOH.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $n(NaOH) = c \times V = 0.20 \times 0.025 = 0.005$ mol
Mark 2: Mole ratio NaOH : HCl = 1 : 1, so $n(HCl)$ required $= 0.005$ mol.
Mark 3: $V(HCl) = n/c = 0.005/0.10 = 0.05$ dm³
Mark 4: $V(HCl) = 50.0$ cm³

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the pH of the 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ HCl solution. (Kw = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: HCl is a strong acid → fully dissociates: $[H^+] = 0.10$ mol·dm⁻³.
Mark 2: $pH = -\log[H^+] = -\log(0.10)$
Mark 3: $pH = 1.00$

subQuestions.questionText: 20.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol·dm⁻³ HCl reacts with 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $n(HCl) = 0.20 \times 0.020 = 0.004$ mol; $n(NaOH) = 0.10 \times 0.020 = 0.002$ mol.
Mark 2: HCl is in excess: $n(HCl)$ remaining $= 0.004 - 0.002 = 0.002$ mol.
Mark 3: Total volume after mixing $= 0.020 + 0.020 = 0.040$ dm³.
Mark 4: $[H^+] = n/V = 0.002/0.040 = 0.05$ mol·dm⁻³.
Mark 5: $pH = -\log(0.05) = 1.30$.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid. Give ONE example of each.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Strong acid — fully (completely) dissociates/ionises in water.
Mark 2: Example of strong acid: HCl (also accept $HNO_3$ or $H_2SO_4$).
Mark 3: Weak acid — only partially dissociates/ionises in water; exists in equilibrium with its undissociated form.
Mark 4: Example of weak acid: $CH_3COOH$ (acetic acid) (also accept $H_2CO_3$, HF, $HCOOH$ etc.).

subQuestions.questionText: A galvanic cell is constructed using zinc (Zn) and copper (Cu) electrodes. Standard electrode potentials: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V; Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. (Refer to the cell diagram in the question paper.) Write down the half-reaction at the ANODE. State whether this is oxidation or reduction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Anode is zinc (more negative $E^\circ$, so it is oxidised).
Mark 2: Half-reaction: $Zn(s) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$.
Mark 3: This is OXIDATION (loss of electrons).

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the half-reaction at the CATHODE. State whether this is oxidation or reduction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Cathode is copper (more positive $E^\circ$, so it is reduced).
Mark 2: Half-reaction: $Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \to Cu(s)$.
Mark 3: This is REDUCTION (gain of electrons).

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the standard cell potential (E°cell) for this cell.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = E^\circ(Cu^{2+}/Cu) - E^\circ(Zn^{2+}/Zn) = +0.34 - (-0.76)$
Mark 2: $E^\circ_{cell} = +1.10$ V

subQuestions.questionText: Write the overall (net) cell reaction.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Reactants and products correct: $Zn(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)$.
Mark 2: Equation balanced (electrons cancel; atoms and charges balance).

subQuestions.questionText: State the function of the salt bridge.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality in both half-cells.
Mark 2: It does so by allowing the migration of ions between the two solutions (e.g. $K^+$ ions move into the cathode compartment and $NO_3^-$ ions move into the anode compartment) to balance any charge build-up. It also completes the circuit.

subQuestions.questionText: In which direction do electrons flow in the external circuit? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Electrons flow from the ZINC electrode (anode) through the external circuit to the COPPER electrode (cathode).
Mark 2: Electrons flow from the electrode with the lower (more negative) reduction potential (Zn, $E^\circ = -0.76$ V) to the electrode with the higher (more positive) reduction potential (Cu, $E^\circ = +0.34$ V).

subQuestions.questionText: What change would you observe at the copper electrode over time? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The copper electrode INCREASES in mass / appears thicker over time.
Mark 2: $Cu^{2+}$ ions in solution accept electrons (reduction): $Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \to Cu(s)$.
Mark 3: Solid copper is deposited on the cathode, so its mass increases. (The blue colour of $CuSO_4$ solution gradually fades as $[Cu^{2+}]$ decreases.)

subQuestions.questionText: Copper(II) sulfate solution (CuSO₄) is electrolysed using copper electrodes. (Refer to the electrolytic cell diagram in the question paper.) Write the half-reaction at the ANODE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Identify oxidation of the copper electrode at the anode (positive electrode in electrolysis).
Mark 2: $Cu(s) \to Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$ (oxidation).

subQuestions.questionText: Write the half-reaction at the CATHODE.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Identify reduction of $Cu^{2+}$ ions at the cathode (negative electrode in electrolysis).
Mark 2: $Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \to Cu(s)$ (reduction).

subQuestions.questionText: What would you observe at each electrode during electrolysis? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Anode — copper electrode DECREASES in mass (dissolves into the solution as $Cu^{2+}$ ions are formed by oxidation).
Mark 2: Cathode — copper electrode INCREASES in mass (solid Cu deposited from reduction of $Cu^{2+}$). The concentration of $CuSO_4$ remains essentially constant because $Cu^{2+}$ produced at the anode equals $Cu^{2+}$ consumed at the cathode.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE industrial application of copper electrolysis.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1-2 (any one valid example): Electrorefining (purification) of impure copper to produce high-purity copper for electrical wiring; OR electroplating of metal objects with a thin layer of copper.
